summary:
Isle of Man stands as a self-legislating Crown Dependency of the United Kingdom with its own parliament, Tynwald. Gender recognition, equality and marriage questions are decided under Manx statutes rather than by automatic application of United Kingdom statutes.

Transgender persons may change legal gender and obtain recognition of the new gender under the Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11).

The Equality Act 2017 lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and ground of non-discrimination alongside age, disability, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. The Act was largely in force from 1 January 2019.

A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and came into effect in 2024.

Same-sex marriage became effective on 22 July 2016 following Royal Assent on 19 July 2016 to the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act. Civil partnerships have been available since 6 April 2011 and could be converted into marriage without a second ceremony, with the first conversion completed within days of entry into force through routine registration.

Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016 records the Legislative Council Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016.
tangentialFactors: In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory and the first part of the British Isles to ban conversion therapy.
localsOnly: Same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint and stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011.
outOfScopeNotes:
A July 2022 community consultation progressed toward a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. It remains unresolved on the sources whether the bill was enacted and what protections, penalties or enforcement it provides.

No sourced information was available on entry or visa rules specific to trans visitors, screening that risks outing, bathroom or facilities law, gender-affirming care access, prison placement practice, hate-crime enforcement outcomes, or trans-specific violence in the Isle of Man.
